title: Maine Football’s Long Season Comes to End with 24-21 Loss to UNH - 92.9 The Ticket

The Black Bears had a chance to tie the game with 56 seconds left, but Omar Aboutoui's 27 yard field goal sailed wide-right. The game had been tied 21-21 when Lucas Glassburn kicked a 44 yard field goal that bounced off the upright and went through for 3 points. Maine took a 7-0 lead with 10 minutes left to play in the 1st Quarter, when Michael McMaugh connected on a 37 yard pass to Ty Boone. The point after was good. UNH tied the game with 4:47 left to play in the 1st Quarter on a 20 yard run by Myles Thomasson . With the extra point good, the game was tied 7-7. Maine took a 14-7 lead with 3:10 left to play in the 1st Quarter. McMaugh connected on a 43 yard pass to Major Leak. The point after was good. The Black Bears led 21-7 with 13:46 left in the 1st Half, on another touchdown pass from McMaugh. This time it was a 30-yarder to Sebastian Ramery. The point after was good. UNH scored two touchdowns to tied the score at 21-21 at the end of the 1st Half. Tommy McLeish connected on a 36 yard pass to Colby Ramshaw and then McLeish connected on a 11 yard pass to Ryan Ricketti. Maine outgained UNH rushing 215-49.UNH had 245 yards passing compared to Maine's 188 yards. Maine outgained UNH 403-294 yards. Michael McMaugh was 10-23 passing for 188 yards and 3 touchdowns. Sebastian Ramery was Maine's leading receiver catching the ball twice for 60 yards. Omar Aboutouni missed 2 field goals for Maine, both from 27 yards in the 4th Quarter. Sam Oppenhimer was Maine's leading tackler with 12 total tackles, 5 solo and 7 assists. UNH ends the season with a 5-7 record and 4-4 in the CAA. title: UNH football beats Maine on late field goal, retains Brice-Cowell Musket - Seacoastonline.com
content: ORONO, Maine – Sophomore Lucas Glassburn kicked the game-winning 44-yard field goal to lift the University of New Hampshire football team to Saturday afternoon’s 24-21 victory against the University of Maine at Alfond Stadium to retain the Brice-Cowell Musket, which is presented annually to the winner of this interstate rivalry game. UNH claimed the Musket for the fifth consecutive year, and the Wildcats have won 14 of the last 16 matchups and 21 of 24 dating back to the 2003 season. UNH sophomore quarterback Tommy McLeish completed 27 of 38 passes for 245 yards, including a 36-yard touchdown to grad student tight end Colby Ramshaw and an 11-yard TD to sophomore wide receiver Ryan Ricketti. Senior wide receiver Ja’Carree Kelly had eight catches for 65 yards, and Ramshaw finished with 48 yards on three receptions and Ricketti had five catches for 42 yards. Grad student Myles Thomason was UNH’s top rusher with 42 yards, and he also had a 39-yard punt return that set up a touchdown. The defensive unit was led by grad student safety Jackson Stone with nine tackles and sophomore linebackers Trevor Barry and Matthew Sopp with eight apiece. Maine was led offensively by Rashawn Marshall’s 164 rushing yards and Michael McMaugh’s three TD passes. Sam Oppenheier led all players with 12 tackles. UNH extended its season-ending win streak to three games to finish at 5-7 overall and 4-4 in the CAA. Maine lost its 10th consecutive game to finish 1-10 overall and 1-7 in the CAA. ORONO — The last thud hurts as much as the first. That was apparent from the look on coach Jordan Stevens’ face as he sat down for his final postgame press conference of the season. The University of Maine football team lost 24-21 to rival New Hampshire on Saturday at Alfond Stadium. The Black Bears end the season with a 1-10 record and 10 losses in a row after opening the season with a promising win at Towson. The 1-10 record is Maine’s worst in 60 years, since a winless season in 1967. No players were made available for Maine’s postgame press conference. Stevens was left to explain the freefall of a season on his own. They could have run a tape of one of his press conferences from earlier in the season. When the losses blur together, themes are repeated. How many times this season did he praise his team’s effort, the good week of practice that led to the same painful result? Executing a game plan for naught? The frustration on Stevens’ face said more than the words he chose. “It doesn’t come down to one play, but it does, at the same time,” Stevens said. Omar Aboutoui missed a pair of 27-yard field goals in the fourth quarter. The first would have given Maine the lead with around six and a half minutes left. The second, with 56 seconds left, secured victory for the Wildcats. Wide receiver Major Leak caught a 43-yard touchdown pass late in the first quarter from Michael McMaugh, Maine’s third starting quarterback of the season. But Leak dropped what would have been a sure touchdown on another long pass in the third quarter, with the game tied at 21-21. That’s 13 potential points floating away like a lost balloon. Good teams find a way to win. Bad teams create ways to lose, often seemingly out of thin air. Ten straight losses is more than enough to move a football team out of the snakebitten, unlucky column and into the bad column. Maine gained 403 yards Saturday, its highest output of the season by 51 yards, but it didn’t change the result. Stevens fired offensive coordinator Mikahael Waters when the Black Bears were 1-5. It didn’t matter. The end zone remained elusive. In the first half Saturday, it looked as if maybe the offense had found something with McMaugh taking snaps. The Black Bears’ first three possessions each ended with a touchdown, first a 37-yard pass to Ty Boone, then a 43-yard pass to Leak, then a 30-yard pass to Sebastian Ramery on an honest-to-goodness double flea flicker. Then the scoring was over for Maine. The Black Bears moved the ball some the rest of the game, but the minor scoring barrage was as complete as the season. An offense that sat among the worst in the Football Championship Subdivision throughout the season found its level. “The roster is not the complete story as to what needs to be assessed,” Stevens said. Break it all down, from head to hoof. Players, coaches, formations, practice habits, film sessions, lunch menus. When you’re 1-10, everything really has to mean everything. Trying to put a brave face on the lost season of 2026, Stevens pointed at the number of young players in the program. The Black Bears played nine freshmen Saturday, he said. Now the recruiting process begins to anew, figuring out which players to keep while bring new recruits into the fold, either from high school or the transfer portal. Maine was an isolated outpost in college football before student athletes had unlimited transfer potential and the ability to earn a paycheck. Those factors make the rebuild ahead of Stevens — who is under contract for two more seasons — that much harder. It’s not a simple fix, either. If it was, losses wouldn’t stack like firewood. Aside from the season-opening victory at Towson, wins were out of reach. Sometimes it was by inches and sometimes by miles, but when the result repeats week after week, what’s the difference? As Maine fans saw all fall, that’s easier said than done. Travis Lazarczyk has covered sports for the Portland Press Herald since 2021. Late on Thursday, November 19, 2026, UnitedHealth Group (NYSE:UNH | UNH Price Prediction) sued the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) in federal court in Brunswick, Georgia. The suit challenges its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings. The company alleges that CMS improperly used 26 measures to rate 45 of its contracts. It says the agency either lacked the legal authority to do so, gave the company no chance to object, or both. UnitedHealth says those contracts would score at least half a star and up to 1.5 stars higher if CMS calculated them correctly. The court has not ruled, and CMS declined to comment. The stock closed Friday, November 20, at $339.85, up 2.84%, while the S&P 500 fell 3.70%. That gain followed a 5.6% drop on Thursday, which came amid concerns about a proposed CMS audit crackdown and Medicare expansion plans. CMS rates plans from 1 to 5 stars, and contracts with at least four stars earn government bonus payments. A half-star swing matters most for a contract sitting just under four stars, because crossing that line unlocks bonus money that pays for richer benefits and lower premiums. The complaint calls the ratings the government’s “principal signal” to patients about plan quality. It warns that low ratings could cut benefits and raise premiums. UnitedHealth said it did not take the step lightly and still wants to work with CMS on the Stars program. The company has disclosed no dollar figure for what it stands to lose. title: UnitedHealth UNH Stock Dives 20% as Breakup Pressure and Medicare Audit Threats Hit the Healthcare Insurers - FXLeaders
content: UnitedHealth UNH stock plunged to $320s as proposed Medicare audit reforms, political calls to break up healthcare conglomerates and rising medical costs threaten insurers’ earnings and margins. Healthcare stocks extended their decline on Wednesday after the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) proposed tougher oversight of Medicare, Medicaid, the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) and the health insurance marketplace. UnitedHealth Group (NYSE: UNH) has been among the hardest hit, falling approximately 20% in three sessions and slipping below $330. Proposed Medicare Advantage audit reforms, political pressure to break up large healthcare conglomerates and rising medical costs are combining to undermine investor confidence in the sector. A major catalyst emerged on November 16, when CMS proposed the Comprehensive Regulations to Uncover Suspicious Healthcare, or CRUSH rule. The proposal would formalise risk-adjustment data validation audits and allow regulators to extrapolate findings from sampled claims across entire Medicare Advantage contracts. Audits could extend back to payment year 2018, with CMS estimating that the framework could recover approximately $9 billion annually across the industry. UnitedHealth faces considerable exposure because it operates the country’s largest Medicare Advantage business. Mizuho analyst Ann Hynes identified UnitedHealth and Humana as the insurers most vulnerable to the proposed changes, followed by CVS Health, Elevance Health, Centene and Molina Healthcare. Political pressure is creating another headwind. Senator Elizabeth Warren has called for breaking up vertically integrated healthcare conglomerates, specifically naming UnitedHealth, CVS and Cigna while supporting the proposed Break Up Big Medicine Act. Restrictions on insurers owning pharmacy benefit managers and healthcare providers could threaten UnitedHealth’s integrated Optum business model. Such measures could limit operational flexibility, increase compliance costs and potentially weaken the advantages of its vertically integrated structure. UnitedHealth shares have come under renewed selling pressure, falling approximately 9% on Wednesday after failing to consolidate gains above $400. The stock has retreated into the $320s, with investors reassessing the regulatory and operational risks facing the managed-care sector. Insurers are also facing elevated medical utilisation, particularly across outpatient and specialty services. If healthcare costs continue rising faster than premiums, underwriting profitability could deteriorate, adding pressure to earnings forecasts. UnitedHealth retains significant scale and cash-flow generation, but the combination of regulatory uncertainty, potential Medicare payment recoveries and higher medical costs leaves its shares vulnerable. Investors will be watching management guidance and the $350 area as an important technical reference, while a sustained recovery will likely require greater clarity on the potential financial impact of the CMS proposal.

title: Huskies Drop Game 1 vs. UNH - University of Connecticut Athletics
content: STORRS, Conn. — UConn men's hockey dropped game one of the two game series vs. New Hampshire by a final of 6-3 Thursday evening. The Huskies scored once in each period and finished with a 25-22 shot advantage, including a power-play goal in the second. UConn opened the first period a man down when Brendan Dunphy was called for a hooking penalty early in the first period. New Hampshire broke through five minutes in when a shot from the point beat Hendrickson. On the ensuing shift, Ethan Gardula found the back of the net following a Joey Muldowney steal, tying the game at one. Following the tie, both teams traded chances, but New Hampshire regained the lead when a save by Hendrickson bounced to a New Hampshire skater who fired it home for the 2-1 lead. The Huskies started the second period strong looking for the equalizer, but New Hampshire defense stayed strong. The Wildcats increased their lead early in the second when the Wildcats beat the Huskies defense creating an odd man rush. The Huskies answered on the power play shortly after when Alexandre Blais fired a one timer cutting the deficit to 3-2. The Huskies increased the pressure and were able to create another power play opportunity, but the Huskies were unable to find the back of the net with the man advantage. With the power play expiring, New Hampshire stole the puck at the blue line, and another odd man rush gave the Wildcats their fourth goal of the night once again giving the Wildcats the two-goal lead. The two teams battled in the third, but New Hampshire found the back of the net first increasing the lead to 5-2. Freshman Lirim Amidovski answered for UConn late in the period cutting the deficit to two. With under three minutes remaining in the game, UConn pulled Hendrickson in favor of an extra skater but with 53 seconds left in the game the Wildcats scored on the empty net securing the 6-3 win. UP NEXT: Huskies will wrap up the two game series Saturday November 21 in New Hampshire. Puck drop is scheduled for 5pm and can be streamed live on ESPN+.

title: UNH Poll Finds Voters Happy With NH Elections, Boosting Case to Keep Scanlan - NH Journal
content: Republican Secretary of State David Scanlan says performance, not partisanship, should be the criteria for filling his office. And new numbers from the UNH Survey Center show Granite Staters are very happy with Scanlan’s performance as the state’s top election official. The latest Granite State Poll, a States of Opinion Project, released Thursday, found 88% of voters said casting a ballot in the Nov. 3 election was “very easy.” That includes 84% of registered Democrats and 89% of undeclared voters. More than half of Granite Staters said voting took them less than 15 minutes on Election Day, and 75% said they were very confident in the accuracy of the vote count. “I believe this information represents that the substantial efforts that my office has been taking to build voter confidence in elections is working,” Scanlan told NHJournal. The findings arrive as Scanlan seeks another term from a legislature transformed from a solid GOP majority to a 292-seat Democratic House supermajority, and a 15-9 majority in the Senate. Lawmakers will elect the secretary of state in a joint session on Organization Day, Dec. 2. Three Democrats have entered the race to replace him: NH-01 candidate and Hampton Select Board Chair Carleigh Beriont; James Butler, who worked for America Votes, a national progressive political organization; and Manchester state Rep. Patrick Long. “I’m seeking this office on the basis of my own record, and it’s a strong one,” Scanlan said Tuesday when announcing his reelection bid. Three prominent Democrats are backing him: former U.S. ambassadors Dick Swett, George Bruno and Terry Shumaker, who served under Democratic presidents. “It would be tragic for New Hampshire if Democrats turned this office into a political football,” they said in a statement Thursday. Political observers say Scanlan holding on to his job is a long shot at best. The warning accompanying their endorsement was blunt. “It would be tragic for New Hampshire if Democrats turned this office into a political football. It’s important not to overreach.” Their support adds to an argument Scanlan and his allies have been making since the election: A change in the legislature’s partisan control should not automatically mean a change in the office responsible for administering elections. The UNH findings offer support for Scanlan’s argument. Among self-identified Democrats who voted, 96% said they were very confident their ballot was counted accurately, with another 3% somewhat confident. Democratic confidence exceeded that of independents and Republicans. Among Republicans, whose party suffered sweeping losses, 54% were very confident and 29% somewhat confident their vote was counted accurately. Among independents, the figures were 59% and 32%, respectively. Scanlan, who became secretary of state in 2022, previously spent two decades as deputy to Democrat Bill Gardner. Gardner held the office for 46 years, surviving changes in legislative control and winning support from both parties. The three Democrats seeking the office are campaigning on pledges to adopt or support new election policies supported by the political left, such as expanded voting by mail and no-excuse absentee balloting. Scanlan’s allies point to his refusal to turn over confidential voter information to President Donald Trump’s Justice Department as evidence of independence from his party. There is also the question of who will defend New Hampshire’s first-in-the-nation presidential primary against pressure from national party leaders. Beriont and Butler have pledged to protect it. Scanlan argues his experience makes him best equipped to withstand that pressure. Former Democratic state Rep. Jim Splaine, who authored the 1975 law protecting the primary’s status, is also backing Scanlan. For Scanlan, the challenge is translating confidence in the elections into votes from Democratic lawmakers. His stated standard for running the office applies regardless of which party controls the State House: “The law is the law.” With progressive politics on the rise, however, that may not be enough.
